tagline.text: A volcanic island in the middle of Laguna de Bay, with a trek up Mount Tagapo

location.label: Location
location.text: Center of Laguna de Bay, between Binangonan and Cardona, Rizal

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–February dry season (boats may be cancelled in the June–October rainy season)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱900–1,500 (per person, covering transport, boat, environmental fee and a shared guide)

children.text: Talim Island is the largest island in Laguna de Bay, the largest lake in the Philippines. It is a day-trip destination where you take a bangka from Binangonan port, climb 438-meter Mount Tagapo and enjoy bamboo villages and lake scenery.

Talim Island is a volcanic island lying almost in the center of Laguna de Bay and is the largest island in the lake. According to Wikipedia, it forms the southwest rim of the caldera, and its northern tip is separated from the mainland by a narrow channel called Diablo Pass. The narrowest point is about

wide, and the southern tip is called Talim Point. The population was about 40,000 in 2020, and there are 24 barangays along the coast: 17 on the west side belong to Binangonan and 7 on the east side to Cardona. The island was formed by volcanic activity, and craters and maars (explosion crater lakes) are described as forming at the southern end after the caldera was created. The largest crater is said to be about
3km
across, surrounding the villages of Balibago and Tuna, but that figure is weakly sourced, so treat it as a reference only. In 1943, during World War II, Marking's Guerrillas operated on the island.
For travelers, the heart of Talim Island is Mount Tagapo. At about

it is the highest point on the island, and the conical hill near the summit is said to resemble a woman's breast, which is why locals also call it "Bundok ng Susong Dalaga" (Maiden's Breast Mountain). The round-trip route is about
6.4km
and gentle, so even first-time hikers can try it. From the top you can look out over Laguna de Bay and the surrounding mountains.

The islanders' main livelihood is making and selling bamboo furniture such as sofas, cabinets, tables and chairs, followed by lake fish farming and fishing. Floating stilt houses used by fish-pen keepers sit on the lake, and in some villages hot groundwater comes out of the ground. Local Filipinos know the island as a place that is close to the mainland yet keeps a slow island atmosphere.

This guide is for travelers who want to take a day to reach Talim Island from Manila or Rizal. You have to take a small boat called a bangka from the mainland, and boats leave only when they fill up, so there is no fixed schedule. Boat fares, last boat times and environmental fees differ slightly between sources, so it is best to confirm them again locally. We recommend leaving very early and returning in the early afternoon.
This is the highest point on the island, and the climb to the summit usually takes
2–2.5 hours
. The descent takes about
1.5 hours
. The trailhead is in Barangay Janosa, and you pass through shaded bamboo forest before grassland appears higher up. The last stretch of about
20 minutes
before the summit has no shade, so prepare for the sun. The route is divided into four sections. The first
1km

from the barangay to the forest entrance is a cement road and flat dirt trail, with the last small stores. The lower forest is a gentle uphill under bamboo shade and is slippery when wet. The upper forest is rocky and steeper, and after the campsite the path to the summit runs through grass.

The boat ride from Binangonan port to the island is a sight in itself. Fish pens, fishing boats and stilt houses line the water, and on clear days you can see mountain ranges in the distance. Because the boat stops at several villages on the island, the trip can take about
1–1.5 hours
. Looking down at the lake from the boat, you will often find morning mist, and the view differs between the outbound and return trips, which makes it good for photos.

Bamboo furniture is an important livelihood for the islanders. As you walk through the villages, you can see people making or drying bamboo sofas and shelves by the roadside. You can look for a small bamboo item as a souvenir. Bamboo furniture is a trade passed down for generations, so it is better to chat and watch how things are made than to haggle over prices.

About 17 villages on the island are reported to be linked by paved roads. If you can rent a bicycle, you can ride through the villages to see lake and field scenery, and some people take on the uphill road toward Mount Tagapo. Ask locally whether bicycles are available and what they cost.

It is reported that you may be served a meal in the stilt houses where fish-farm owners stay. Ask your boatman for an introduction and agree on a price in advance. This is not an organized product, so some days it will not be possible.

blocks.title: Hot spring water on Talim Island

children.text: Hot groundwater is reported in the villages of Tabon and Binitigan. It is not a developed facility like the hot spring resorts in Pansol, so lower your expectations and drop in casually.
Greenpeace reported about 181 bird species around Laguna de Bay. Herons, kingfishers and flowerpeckers are known to live there, so a pair of binoculars lets you enjoy birdwatching even from the boat.

items.title: Mount Tagapo day plan
items.subtitle: From the port to the summit

children.text: Leave Manila and take a UV Express to Binangonan from the terminal at Starmall EDSA-Shaw.
Arrive at Pritil Port in Binangonan and buy drinks, snacks and water.
Take a bangka to Barangay Janosa.
Register near the Janosa barangay hall, pay the environmental fee and get a guide assigned.
Start the trek through bamboo forest and grassland.
Enjoy the lake views from the summit.
Begin the descent.
Come down to the village, have lunch and check the last boat time.
Take a bangka back to Binangonan.
When you register at Janosa, it is safer to leave your contact details and expected return time. If you miss the last boat you will have to sleep on the island, so come down in the early afternoon.
Take a boat from Binangonan port to a village on the island.
Walk village lanes to see bamboo furniture workshops and lake views.
Have lunch in a stilt house or village eatery.
Agree on a time with your boatman and return to the port.
This is not an organized product, so agree on the schedule and fare with the boatman in advance.
Take a UV Express to Binangonan from the terminal in front of Starmall EDSA-Shaw. The fare is reported at about
From Cubao, take a jeepney to Binangonan near Farmers Market or Ali Mall and get off near Pritil Port.
From the Binangonan junction, a tricycle to Pritil Port costs about
One source says it takes about
2 hours
from Ortigas or Cubao to the port.
If you drive, search Waze for Binangonan Fishport. All fares are from published sources, so confirm them locally.

items.title: Getting to the island by boat

children.text: Take a bangka from Binangonan port to Barangay Janosa. The round trip is reported at about
and takes 1–1.5 hours.
Boats leave when they fill up, so there is no fixed time, and the last boat is between 4:30 and 6 PM depending on the source.
A chartered boat is reported at about
The Janosa barangay hall is close to the landing, and you register next to the basketball court near the hall. Registration usually takes under
15 minutes
, and no online pre-registration or separate permit is reported to be needed.
A 2017 source describes 30–90 minutes from the port depending on the village and fares of 15–60 pesos. These differ greatly by season, so confirm locally.
It is reported that boats to the island also leave from Cardona port (Santos Street, Patunhay).
Jeepneys from EDSA Crossing and Starmall to Tanay pass through Cardona.
Both trekking and boats are easiest in the dry season, November to February. If you climb for sunrise, you avoid the sun.

In the rainy season (June–October) the mountain trail is slippery with mud and waves can be high, so boats may stop running on some days. From March to May the sun is strong, so an early start is essential.

The island lies on the lake, so the wind is stronger than on land, and on foggy days the lake view may be hidden. If it rained the day before, ask your guide about trail conditions before you set out.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Best time for trekking. A sunrise hike is also pleasant.
The summit has no shade, so prepare water and sun protection.
Muddy trail and possible boat cancellations. Check the weather before you leave.

items.label: Meals and snacks
items.note: Small stores and eateries on the island

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

The island has small stores and eateries, but the choice is limited, so it is safer to prepare water and snacks in Binangonan or Manila. There is nowhere on the trail to buy water. For lunch, you can eat at a store in Barangay Janosa or in a stilt house on the lake.

A day trip is the norm, and the camping area is 10–15 minutes below the summit. A separate fee is reported for camping, so check at the barangay hall. On the mainland, Antipolo and Angono are the closest places to stay.

Barangay Janosa is the village on the island that travelers visit most, and registration, meals and guide assignment all take place here. Remember how much environmental fee you paid, and ask for a receipt if you need one.
Leaving at 4–5 AM and catching an early-morning bangka is the safest plan.
Bring at least 2 liters of water per person, and up to 3 liters in summer.
Wear hiking boots or shoes with good grip, and trekking poles help in the rainy season.
Register at the Janosa barangay hall and leave your contact details and expected return time.
Toilets are only near the trailhead, so use them before you set out.
Boats leave only when full, so a small group may have to wait.
The last boat time varies by season, so ask the boatman as soon as you arrive.
Children aged 7 and older are reported to be able to climb with adult supervision.
Guides are assigned in turn at the barangay hall, and advance booking is reported to be discouraged.
Mobile signal works on most of the trail, but emergency response on the island is slow, so tell family or friends your plans.
Boats leave without a fixed schedule only when full, and if you miss the last boat you will have to stay overnight on the island, so return in the early afternoon.
Swimming in Laguna de Bay is not recommended because of pollution and fish pens.
In the rainy season the trail is slippery and boats may be cancelled, so check the weather.
Emergency response on the island is slower than on the mainland. Bring your own basic medicines.
The summit stretch has no shade, so watch out for heat illness.
Fees and rules differ between sources, so confirm them directly at the barangay hall and with the boatmen.
An arts town close to Binangonan on the mainland side, you can visit it along the route near the lake.

blocks.title: Tanay Old Town and San Ildefonso Church

children.text: A lakeside old town you reach by driving along East Road from Cardona. You can link villages and churches on the east side of the lake into a full-day plan.
A windmill landmark on the lake's eastern shore that is easy to combine in the same regional itinerary.
A Rizal city where you can stop for a meal or views on your way back to Manila.
